units.translation: 917. Erycos medeousa: Eryx is the name of a city, where Aphrodite is honored; others say Sicily.
920. 〈opazon:〉 they pursued. Sᵐ
921. mixodiēisin halos: he calls the place mixodia, where Scylla and Charybdis were, because they are opposite each other.
923. amoton: unceasing. Lᴳ P
926. pyrithalpeos: of that which is burned by fire. Lᵐ (P)
936. parboladēn: in an interjected manner. Lᵐ (P)
937. epētrimoi: swimming from the sides or together towards each other on both sides.
940-42a. autik’ anaschome〈nai〉: immediately drawing up their garments onto their white knees and fastening them with their girdle, they moved vigorously above the rocks and the breaking of the wave.
b. 〈agē: it is written〉 augē. Sᵐ
947a. ērēreinto: they were approaching, they were settling. Lᵐ (P)
b. 〈kyma:〉 it is written oidma. Gᴳ
954. [tēn de parēoriēn] 〈diēeriēn〉: aloft; for the Nereids were carrying her above the rocks, tossing her to one another like a ball.
957. orthos epi steleē: steleē is the handle, typides are the hammer's head; leaning on the wood of the hammer.
960. 〈balle:〉 he struck. Sᵐ
961. hossē d’ eiarinou: as much as is the interval of a spring day and hour; instead of interval 〈portion and〉 share. He has called the equinox a spring day.

965. Thrinakiēs leimō〈na〉: Timaeus (fg 1 M. I 193) says that Sicily is called Thrinacia because it has three promontories; but the historians say that Thrinacus ruled Sicily 〈...〉 and Mylae is a peninsula of Sicily, where the cattle of Helios grazed.
972a. argyreon chaion: a chaion is a curved staff, which shepherds use; but Amerias rendered it as a bare rod. Callimachus (fg 125 Schn. = 4 Kapp):

‘a broad veil extending from your head suited you, a shepherd's felt cap’ and holding a chaion in your hand. And the word erysichaion in Alcman (fg 24 B. III 45), drawing and shepherding with the chaion. pēchynousa instead of having attached to the forearm of the hand.
b. 〈chaion:〉 a shepherd's staff. Sᵐ

973. oreichalkoio pha〈einou〉: oreichalkos is a kind of bronze, named from a certain Oreius who was its discoverer. But Aristotle in the Teletai (fg 10 Rose Arist. pseudep. 1863, 619) says that neither the name nor its kind exists; for some suppose that oreichalkos is spoken of, but does not exist. And this is one of the things spread at random; for the more inquisitive say that it exists. Stesichorus (fg 88 B. III 231) and Bacchylides (fg 68 B. III 588 = 51 Blass-Snell) also mention it, and the grammarian Aristophanes (fg 79 Nauck) has noted this. Others say it is the name of a sculptor, as Socrates (fg 18 M. IV 500) and Theopompus in the 25th book (115 fg 158 J.). Thus it was in the Comic Lexicon, the mixed one (Didymi fg I 5, 34 a Schmidt 70).
